videos.transcript_text:
The 6th generation VW Golf is a perfect daily driver,
until one of the magnificent tsi engines break.
But let’s not overtake the things which 
should not be overtaken.
This Mk6 Golf is just sort of a facelift of the older Mk5 since 
they share the same platform and what not.
Besides the 3 or 5 door hatchback there is also 
the more practical wagon,
if you need that extra space for your dog, fridge, oven or wardrobe and what not.
There is also the convertible, the Jetta and the Golf plus, but I’m not going to mention these anymore,
because the universe would not handle that much information.
The interior of this Golf is a typical Golf interior, so it can be equipped poorly but also pretty damn well
other than this:
-the build quality is good, although some rattles can occur mainly from the doors or B pillar area
-the space is good, although it’s still a small car so don’t expect miracles
-the materials quality is good, although there are occasionally cases of sagging headliner in cars used in hot climate areas
-and lastly the ergonomics is great, but there are more important things to mention so for more information about the interior visit my website.
Overall the body is protected well from the rust, however on cars used regularly on winter salty roads,
it’s definitely worth to check for rust on 3 places:
-the front fenders can rust
-the front edge of the sills can rust, because over time dirt builds up in this area behind the wheel well liner
-and lastly there is the tailgate which can rust mostly around 
the 3rd brake light, but sometimes on the edges, around the middle drain hole
+ occasionally around the VW badge too, so basically check the whole damn tailgate for rust!
But let’s move on to the minor issues unrelated to engine or gearbox,
so: -the trunk door lock can fail more often causing the trunk door not to lock properly, or it will be stuck in closed position
-excessive tail light condensation can occur too, in the outer as well as in inner tail lights
-then there is the AC system which you should check properly since:
the AC compressor clutch hub can wear out,
the AC condenser can leak more often,
the blower motor resistor can fail
and the air recirculation flap motor located behind the glove box can break too.
Then of course check the functionality of the other regular stuff like the power windows, door locks, rear and front windscreen wipers and all that other shit as usual.
For more information and for guides how to fix these issues visit my website!
As the other cars, this Golf can also have issues with various water leaks into the interior,
so check the footwell area and the trunk spare tire area for traces of water.
There are numerous sources of water leaks, but let’s start with the rear of the car, specifically with the tailgate,
so:  -the inner tail light seals can let the water in
+ in this case there should be a visible condensation in them
-next the 3rd brake light can let the water in
-then occasionally the draining tube of the rear badge can be dislodged and drain the water into the trunk
+let’s not forget the plastic washer fluid pipe which can crack,
usually in this wiring loom rubber grommet and in this case it obviously leaks washer fluid into the interior or into the tailgate.
Moving on to the front of the car:
-the 2 water drains under the windshield on the sides of the scuttle area can be clogged letting the water to accumulate here,
and leak into the interior thru the plastic air inlet.
-then the ac drain in the front right footwell can leak
-and also the rear windscreen washer plastic pipe can crack and leak washer fluid,
again in the front right passenger footwell area.
Additionally if the car is equipped with a sunroof then you can easily get another leak from the sunroof drains.
There are 4 drain hoses in each corner of the sunroof frame.
The rear drain hoses are usually fine, but the front drain hose rubber endings can be often clogged.
To access these drain endings you have to remove the windscreen wipers and the plastic panel,
since the front drain hoses drain the water into this scuttle area.
However sometimes the drain hose can also disconnect from this rubber grommet
which goes thru the firewall-and in this case you 
again end up with water in the front footwell.
But I’m not finished yet, since the estate models 
can be equipped with a big panoramic sunroof
which also has 4 drains. But in this case you can 
easily get a leak from all of these drain hoses,
since all of them have badly designed upper drain 
connections.
These connectors glued to these hoses simply get a little loose over time creating a gap around the hose which allows the water to leak not just into,
but also onto the drain hose and into the interior.
+ of course the front drains can  get clogged the same way as on the regular sunroof.
This Golf was available with the standard suspension, with the factory sport suspension or with the electronically adjustable suspension.
As always check for all those knocking, 
clunking or rattling noises from the suspension
and keep in mind that the electronic shocks are 
obviously more expensive than the regular type.
From the petrol engines the most reliable are the 
older 1.4 l and 1.6 l naturally aspirated units.
They are not very powerful and also not 
that economical as the newer engines,
but they can easily withstand 300 000 km or 
more with regular maintenance only.
However it’s worth mentioning that after approx. 200 
000 km or 250 000 km you can experience bigger or smaller oil consumption.
+ of course let’s not forget about the 2.5 l 5 cylinder engine available in the US,
which is also a great, reliable and a fairly simple unit,
so all I can say is: Buy it if you can!
But from now on it’s going to be nothing but downhill on a highway to hell…
So let me introduce you the newer TSI- totaler, schrottmotor inclusive,
turbocharged and direct injection engines which are powerful enough while achieving a good fuel consumption,
But they can have numerous, numerous issues:
-let’s start with the 1.2 l TSI
The biggest issue of this smallest engine can be with the timing chain mechanism which is made from boiled potatoes basically.
It’s because in plenty of cases it was and it can 
be worn even before 100 000 km, and in fact
The next problem of this tiny engine can be with the faulty turbo wastegate actuator,
but in this case the actuator arm can be only stuck, so before replacing the actuator itself,
its worth to first disassemble the actuator and try to free up the things.
The last issue worth mentioning is that this engine is more prone to oil dilution with fuel.
So if you will use this engine for very short distances only, then you can experience that the fuel will slowly get into the oil
which is not very good in the long term.
-the 1.4 l TSI with 122 hp is on the other hand a much better engine,
but even this unit can have issues with the prematurely worn timing chain.
In this case you can expect this issue mostly between 
100 000 km and 150 000 km. However,
in some cases the chain mechanism can be worn even before 100 000 km, but again mostly in the cars made to 2011.
-next there is the infamous 1.4 l TSI with 160 hp,
which is equipped with a turbocharger and also with a compressor to achieve the very good performance.
But the various possible issues of this engine are not that good as the performance.
And again let’s start with the damn timing chain, which as in the previous engine can be worn mostly between 100 000 km and 150 000 km,
but there are also cases of worn chain mechanism even before 100 000 km mainly in cars made to 2011.
The next issue of this engine is related to the compressor, specifically to the magnetic clutch of the compressor,
which can fail even before 100 000 km causing weak engine performance,
since the compressor is not gonna be to be engaged.
In this case you will have to replace this clutch which is connected to the water pump.
But let’s move onto the most interesting issue this engine can have which is related to the pistons.
Specifically the side of the pistons can crack
and also break off basically, even before 100 000 km.
This will cause misfires because of low compression, excessive oil consumption, a check engine light can be also present of course,
and also some other funny shit.
Replacing the pistons and all the other necessary stuff is obviously expensive,
so I would not recommend choosing this engine 
if you don’t have the extra money to fix this.
I mean you can buy it, but I would rather a buy a cement mixer or something.
-Next there is the GTI version equipped with a 2.0 l TSI engine which can have a couple of problems as well.
In this case again the damn timing chain mechanism can be a bit problematic,
specifically the very first weaker version of the timing chain tensioner can fail,
and damage your engine even before 100 000 km.
since there is a noticeable difference between the old and the updated tensioner.
-the next problematic part of this engine is called the camshaft bridge
which can occasionally cause oil starvation in the cylinder head or other damage if this small screen falls out from it.
The good thing is that only the cars made to 2009 are more prone to this,
since they have the earliest version of the camshaft bridge.
But the bad things is,
that the cam bridge was revised more than 3 times so the screen can fall out on later cars as well.
After this, there is the plastic variable intake manifold 
which can be faulty.
This is a complex plastic garbage with moving plastic flaps in it which can wear out and fail and shit
+ it can also cause  vacuum leaks, so be prepared to replace it with a newer, better and more sturdy updated manifold.
Next there is the PCV valve which can be often faulty before 80 000 mi.
It’s good to replace it preventively since it can blow the rear main seal which starts to leak oil
and that’s an expensive repair.
-before I move onto the most powerful versions, I have to mention the infamous 1.8 l TSI which was interestingly also available in this Golf even though it’s not very common.
This is the same engine which was available in the Audi A4 B8,
and it also has the same common problems as the already mentioned 2.0 l GTI engine.
But except all these issues it also has a very high chance of excessive oil consumption because of the undersized pistons,
piston rings and oil scraper rings.
-lastly there is the Golf GTI edition 35 and the Golf  R both equipped with an older generation 2.0 l TSI engine.
This unit has indeed an older construction but it’s also more reliable than the engine in the regular GTI.
It’s mainly because it has a timing belt instead of a timing chain and it also has a slightly different - better intake manifold.
From the weak points of this engine, the only thing worth mentioning is the HPFP camshaft follower
which you should check / eventually replace since it can get worn and cause issues in the future.
To finally end this journey of engine hell,
I have to mention that all of the direct injection petrol engines can have often issues with leaking water pump so check the coolant level regularly
+ let’s not forget about the other possible issues of these fantastic engines like the:
carbon build up, faulty injectors, faulty ignition coils or  occasionally bigger or smaller oil consumption.
All of the diesel engines can easily reach 300 000 km or 400 000 km,
but of course they can have the regular diesel engine problems which can occur much earlier.
-So the EGR valve can be faulty which is not like the end of the world, but replacing it is not that easy and not that cheap since it’s mounted on the back of the engine
-then the injectors can be faulty usually just after 200  000 km, but occasionally even before 200 000 km or at around this mileage more often on the 1.6 l TDI
-next, the bosch CP4 high pressure fuel pump can fail and in this case it will release
tiny metal particles in the whole fuel system which will destroy the injectors too.
This issue can occur for the most part only in the US or in some parts of Eastern EU,
because of the different quality of the fuel, but even here it’s not like extremely common and if you will practice
these things then you can minimize the possibility of this issue.
-after this it’s good to mention the infamous emission 
scandal and the associated software update
which should correct the emissions, because 
some owners experienced these strange issues
after this update. But the good thing is that because of this emission scandal,
there still should be an extended warranty in the US for 
all the main parts of the diesel engines.
Lastly if you are buying one of the more powerful 
2.0 l TDI engine made to 2009 which has this,
or this engine code then at approx. 200 000 km it’s a good idea
to remove the oil pan and check the oil pump drive shaft which can be worn out and later cause loss of oil pressure which is not good.
All the petrol engines are equipped with a timing chain except the older 1.4 l and the 1.6 l naturally aspirated engines which have a timing belt.
As I already said,
the chain mechanism in the 4 cylinder engines can be worn anytime basically, so even before 100 000 km.
That’s why the best is to either measure how much is it worn or to replace it preventively after buying mainly in the early engines made to mid 2011.
Because keep in mind that if the chain skips then it can easily damage the engine pretty badly.
This VW can be equipped with the 5  or 6 speed manual gearbox or there are three types of automatic transmissions.
-The manual transmissions are usually reliable 
just check them for strange noises and it’s good
to occasionally replace the oil in them. The Dual 
mass flywheel can be of course worn
if the car is equipped with it, but it usually wears out just around 200 000 km, even though
this mostly depends on how the previous owner used the car.
-From the automatic transmissions the regular 6 speed Tiptronic is the most reliable, but sadly this gearbox was mated only to the 2.5 l 5 cylinder petrol engine
-On the other side, the 6 and 7 speed DSG dual clutch gearboxes are not that reliable.
Especially the 7 speed version can have often issues with the mechatronic
and also the clutches can wear out even before 
100 000 km.
+ the DSG gearbox also has a dual mass flywheel which can be worn so keep extra money for the DSG issues
and for more information about these transmissions check out my website!
If you are buying a model equipped with the 4motion 4wd system then make sure that the 4wd is working properly
–so check for front wheel spin since the haldex pump can fail and if it fails then the car is going to be just front wheel drive.
Because of this it’s really important to change the oil in the differential every 50 000 or max 60 000 km
and also change the filter in it which can clog and cause premature failure of the already mentioned haldex pump.
To summarize things up: -the older naturally aspirated petrol engines are the most reliable
-avoid the DSG gearbox unless you have additional 2 000 € to fix it
-avoid cars with performance upgrades and with questionable 
maintenance history
+ keep at least 1000 € for the maintenance and possible repairs, but if you are buying a car with a direct injection petrol engine
or with a diesel engine then keep at least 2000 €, 
and to top of that if you want the more powerful
1.4 tsi twincharger or the GTI model then keep at 
least 3 000€
And as always if you have personal  experience with this car or more information about it, then you can write it into comments!
